The project can be checked for validity to identify potential problems that would prevent the workflows from being executed: does every reference resolve, are no required fields missing, are there any duplicated ids, etc. `validateProject()` does this and prints a readable report. This guide shows how to run it, read the report, act on a problem, and stop a script when the project has a blocking problem.

It assumes you know what a Project is and how to create one (see `vignette("how-to-set-up-a-project")` and `vignette("how-to-design-scenarios")`).

The article uses these functions:

| Function | What it does |
|---|---|
| `validateProject()` | Checks the whole project and returns a report of critical errors and warnings. |
| `isAnyCriticalErrors()` | Returns `TRUE` when a report has at least one critical error. |
| `validationSummary()` | Counts the critical errors and warnings in a report and names the sections that have them. |
| `loadProject()` | Warns about most references to a definition that does not exist, for example a misspelled individual id in a scenario. |
| `validate` argument of `runScenarios()`, `buildSimulations()`, `createDataCombined()` and `createPlots()` | With `TRUE` (the default), the function checks the parts of the project it uses before it runs. With `FALSE`, it skips the check. `runPI()` always checks. |

You should run a validation after you finish editing the project and before running. `runScenarios()`, `buildSimulations()`, `createDataCombined()`, `createPlots()` and `runPI()` each check the parts of the project they use before any simulation starts, and stop with a list of every critical error they find there. They do not show warnings, and they do not look at the other parts of the project. An explicit `validateProject()` gives you the whole picture: every section, warnings included. `vignette("about-the-project-model")` covers more details.

If you want to follow the examples of this article, create a local copy of the example project:

```{r}
project_dir <- withr::local_tempdir()
initProject(destination = project_dir, type = "example", createExcel = FALSE)
project <- loadProject(file.path(project_dir, "Project.json"))
```

Calling `validateProject()` on a `Project` creates a report that lists two kinds of problems:

- **Critical errors** must be fixed. Examples are an id used twice, a required field left empty, or a reference to a definition that does not exist. Until you fix them, the functions that use that part of the project refuse to run.
- **Warnings** do not stop anything. Read them anyway: some point to a problem that only shows up when you run, such as a model file that cannot be found.

To check in a script whether anything blocks, call `isAnyCriticalErrors()`. It returns `TRUE` when the report has at least one critical error.

## Validate a clean project

The example project has no problems. `validateProject()` checks every part of the project, and the references between the parts, then prints a summary of what it found:

```{r}
results <- validateProject(project)
results
```

`isAnyCriticalErrors()` agrees:

```{r}
isAnyCriticalErrors(results)
```

## Find a reference to a missing definition

The most common problem is a reference to a definition that does not exist, usually because an id is misspelled. `addScenario()` refuses such a reference right away. A project loaded from disk can still contain one, for example after someone edited a definition file by hand: `loadProject()` opens the project anyway, so you can repair it (`vignette("about-the-project-model")` explains why).

As an example, change the individual id `adult_male` to `adlt_male` in one scenario file of the example project, as a hand edit could. `loadProject()` warns about the misspelling when it reads the file:

```{r, warning = TRUE}
scenario_file <- file.path(
  project_dir,
  "definitions",
  "scenarios",
  "aciclovir_iv.json"
)
text <- readLines(scenario_file)
text <- gsub('"adult_male"', '"adlt_male"', text, fixed = TRUE)
writeLines(text, scenario_file)

broken <- loadProject(file.path(project_dir, "Project.json"))
```

The problems can be diagnosed also after loading the project:


```{r}
broken_results <- validateProject(broken)
broken_results
```

## Read a warning

As an example of a warning, set the model file of a scenario to a file that is not in the project's model folder:

```{r}
setScenario(project, "aciclovir_iv", modelFile = "Aciclovir_v2.pkml")
validateProject(project)
```

The report shows one warning and no critical errors. `isAnyCriticalErrors()` returns `FALSE`, so `runScenarios()` starts, but the scenario then fails because the model file cannot be found. Set the correct file name again:

```{r}
setScenario(project, "aciclovir_iv", modelFile = "Aciclovir.pkml")
```

Some warnings are normal. A new, empty project created with `initProject(type = "minimal")` gives one warning for each empty section, for example `No scenarios defined`. The warning goes away when you add a definition to that section.

## Read the result of validation

`validateProject()` returns the report as an R list, so a script can check it without reading the printed text. The list has one element for each section of the project, such as `scenarios` or `individuals`, plus `crossReferences`. `crossReferences` holds the references between definitions that point to something that does not exist. That is why the misspelled individual id is listed there, and not under `scenarios`:

```{r}
names(broken_results)
broken_results$crossReferences$critical_errors[[1]]$message
```

Each element holds the critical errors and warnings of its section. `validationSummary()` counts them for the whole project and names the sections that have any, for example for a status line in a log file:

```{r}
validationSummary(broken_results)
```

## Fix the problem and check again

Fix the problem with the same functions you use to build a project. Here, set the individual of the scenario back to `adult_male`. `setScenario()` changes the project in your R session only. Call `saveProject()` to write the fix to the project files, if needed:

```{r}
setScenario(broken, "aciclovir_iv", individual = "adult_male")
```

Validate again to check that the problem is gone:

```{r}
fixed_results <- validateProject(broken)
fixed_results
isAnyCriticalErrors(fixed_results)
```

The report is clean: every reference points to an existing definition, and no required field is empty. Validation does not load and inspect the model files, so some problems show up only when a scenario is built:

- a parameter path that does not exist in the model
- a model file that cannot be found (a warning only, see above)
- a human individual or population without a PK-Sim population
- a protein ontogeny that cannot be applied
- a human individual used with a model built for an animal

## Stop a script when the project has a blocking problem

In a script that runs without you watching it, for example overnight, validate the project first. If it has a critical error, print the report and stop:

```{r}
results <- validateProject(project)
if (isAnyCriticalErrors(results)) {
  print(results)
  stop("Fix the project before running it.")
}
```

`runScenarios()`, `buildSimulations()`, `createDataCombined()` and `createPlots()` have an argument `validate`. With `validate = FALSE` they skip their own check. `runPI()` always checks.

Skipping the check does not make the problem go away. With the misspelled individual id from above, `runScenarios(project, validate = FALSE)` still runs the scenario. It then uses the individual stored in the model file instead of `adult_male`, and tells you only in a warning:

```
Scenario "aciclovir_iv": No individual characteristics for individual id "adlt_male" found.
```

Use `validate = FALSE` only when you know why the check fails and are sure the results are still correct.

## Where to go next

With a clean project in hand, see `vignette("how-to-run-simulations")` to execute the scenarios and `vignette("how-to-plot-results")` to turn the results into figures. To write or repair the definitions a validation problem points at, see `vignette("how-to-design-scenarios")`.

To look up which fields a definition requires, see `vignette("reference-definition-fields")`. For why validation reports two levels and checks a different slice of the project per entry point, see `vignette("about-the-project-model")`.
